title: Vote for Me (Here's Why)
coreMove: Listen for what a reason is trying to sell and whom it is trying to recruit.
sourcePressure: The chapter moves from private moral justification to public persuasion, ally recruitment, reputation defense, and political-style explanation.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer treats persuasion as manipulation rather than social reasoning aimed at allies, identity, and reputation.

sourceAnchors.name: Vote for Me (Here's Why)
sourceAnchors.detail: the official index title frames the chapter's shift from private justification into public persuasion.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A reason often behaves like a campaign slogan: it is less a microscope than a handbill for the side already chosen.

sourceAnchors.name: the social persuasion framing
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar says the chapter moves from internal justification to recruiting allies and selling positions.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Once the argument enters a room with other people, the reason starts doing reputation work as well as truth work.

hook: Do not open ch04 with a person discovering that morality is complicated.
Do not use 'you think X, but actually Y' as the hook shell.
counterintuition: Avoid treating the opposing view as stupid before explaining the mechanism.
tryThisNow: No generic write down your values prompt.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: city zoning hearing where neighbors cite safety to protect parking
exampleSpecs.audience: planners reading moral rhetoric in public comments
exampleSpecs.stakes: Megan maps each stated reason to the constituency it reassures.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Megan groups comment cards by the audience they signal to, not by the literal topic line.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A stack of comment cards leans against a cracked microphone base.

exampleSpecs.domain: startup founder explaining a pivot to employees and investors
exampleSpecs.stakes: Daniel separates the reason that persuades staff from the reason that reassures investors.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Daniel draft two versions and circle the sentence that protects his status more than the truth.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You see the investor deck and the all-hands notes open on the same laptop.

exampleSpecs.domain: union local choosing language for a contract rejection
exampleSpecs.stakes: Catarina rewrites a technical wage argument as a loyalty appeal to members.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Catarina asks which sentence will make a wavering member feel seen by the group.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Nobody chants a spreadsheet," Catarina says, tapping the wage table.

exampleSpecs.domain: school board candidate responding to a curriculum rumor
exampleSpecs.audience: campaign volunteers tempted by fact dumps
exampleSpecs.stakes: Devon hears the reply as an audition for trust, not only an answer to a rumor.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Devon marks which sentence would recruit anxious parents instead of humiliating them.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Devon one canvassing shift to see that the fact sheet was losing the porch.

exampleSpecs.domain: restaurant group defending a service charge policy
exampleSpecs.stakes: Olivier identifies which reason is for guests and which is for staff pride.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Olivier asks the manager to say the staff-facing reason aloud before writing the menu note.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The receipt printer spits out a test check with the new service charge circled.

exampleSpecs.domain: research lab deciding how to announce a failed replication
exampleSpecs.stakes: Anya distinguishes the public reason from the status-saving reason in the draft statement.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Which sentence in Anya's draft tells the truth, and which one is campaigning for the lab?
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Which sentence would you keep if nobody knew your name was on the paper?

skillTargets: infer the audience a reason is trying to recruit
distinguish private explanation from public persuasion
see reputation defense inside a moral argument

tryThisNowSpec: Before replying to one argument, name the audience the speaker seems to be persuading, even if you are the only visible listener.
